summary.name: Principles of Chaos Engineering
summary.one_liner: A web page laying out the principles of Chaos Engineering, a discipline of running controlled experiments on distributed systems to build confidence in how they withstand turbulent conditions in production.
keywords: how to test distributed system failures
use_cases: Designing experiments to find weaknesses in distributed systems
Deciding how to inject real-world failures such as crashed servers or severed networks
Defining steady-state metrics like error rates and latency percentiles
Limiting customer impact when testing in production
summary.what_it_does: The page defines Chaos Engineering as experimenting on a system to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions in production. It describes a four-step experiment process: define a measurable steady state, hypothesize it continues in control and experimental groups, introduce real-world variables such as server crashes or network failures, and try to disprove the hypothesis. It then lists advanced principles: building hypotheses around steady-state output, varying real-world events, running experiments in production, automating experiments to run continuously, and minimizing blast radius. It gives examples of systemic weaknesses such as improper fallbacks, retry storms, overloaded downstream dependencies, and cascading failures.
notable: Defines the four-step chaos experiment process built on steady-state hypotheses
Recommends experimenting directly on production traffic
Emphasizes minimizing blast radius of experiments
Last updated 2019 March per the page
caveats: This is a set of principles, not a software tool; no specific product or platform is named
Page is a conceptual manifesto and does not describe implementation details or tooling
